title: Bangla Sahib
hookLine: in Delhi, the gurdwara of the child Guru, with its healing pool

lines: A BOTTLE ON A KITCHEN SHELF.
KEPT FOR WHEN SOMEONE IS UNWELL.
FILLED AT A POOL IN DELHI.
cards: A plastic bottle, the kind you'd buy at any corner shop, sits on a kitchen shelf in a Delhi apartment. Nobody drinks from it casually.

It was filled at the edge of a pool in the middle of the city, carried home on the metro, and kept for when someone in the house is unwell. A grandmother pours a little into a steel cup and hands it over without a word.
The pool is at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, near one of the city's big traffic circles. Year one told how the child Guru came to Delhi. Today, the place he left behind, and the water.

teach.b: First, the house. Bangla means bungalow. Tradition says Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru and still a child, stayed here in the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh when he was called to Delhi.
While he was there, an epidemic swept the city, and the child went out among the sick of every faith. He caught the disease himself and died in Delhi. The bungalow became a gurdwara.
Second, the water. Tradition says the house's well gave the water the young Guru blessed and handed to the sick.

teach.h: A POOL FOR THOSE WHO ARE UNWELL.
teach.b: Today a wide pool, a sarovar, lies beside the gurdwara, and people sit by it, touch the water to their eyes, and fill bottles to take home.
Some Sikhs add a caution: the water isn't a charm; what it carries is the memory of a child who served. Third, a hymn.
In Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan gives thanks, in paraphrase: the Beloved has given protection from smallpox; the Supreme Lord has shown mercy.

teach.h: GURU ARJAN'S THANKS FOR A SICK CHILD.
teach.b: Tradition links that hymn to Guru Arjan's young son, the boy who would become Guru Hargobind, when he fell ill. So, as tradition reads it, the Granth holds a father's relief over a sick child.
At Bangla Sahib the story turns around: here it's the child who goes to the sick.

teach.h: THE LIGHT IN A SMALL BODY.
teach.b: Fourth, Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru, whatever the body's age.
At Bangla Sahib you can see what that light did in a small body: it didn't hide from a sick city.

how: Visitors to Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, eat in the langar, and sit by the sarovar; some take its water home for family members who are unwell.

games.q: you're the child Guru, staying in a raja's house in Delhi. an epidemic is spreading through the city. what do you do?
o: stay inside the bungalow until it passes.
go out among the sick of every faith.
games.why: tradition says he went out among the sick, Hindu and Muslim alike, and gave them water. he caught the disease himself and died in Delhi.

practice: See the wide water, the white building and the gold dome, the steps going down to the edge, and people sitting quietly, someone filling a bottle for a person at home.
Now bring to mind one person you know who is unwell, and sit beside them in your mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Bangla Sahib. The gurdwara in Delhi at the bungalow where tradition says Guru Har Krishan stayed and served the sick, with its pool beside it. Today's word.

orig.note: bangla, a bungalow; sahib, a word of honor added to the names of gurdwaras.

carryVoice: Your line: the child's gurdwara. The pool still holds the memory of a child who went to the sick. That's today's step.
